intro: A connector opens the second sentence and tells the listener, before any content arrives, how it relates to the first: more of the same, the opposite of what you expected, the result, a choice between two, or a change of topic. Picture a road sign at the start of sentence two. To choose, ignore English 'and', 'but' and 'so' and ask one question: what does sentence two do to sentence one?

skills.rule: そして and それから add the next event or item (それから stresses 'after that'); それに and その上 add one more point in the same direction ('besides', 'on top of that').
skills.explain:
そして is the neutral 'and' between sentences: the next event, or the next fact in a description. それから is 'and then, after that': it puts the second event later in time, and in speech it also tacks one more item onto a list (卵と牛乳、それからパンも).

それに and その上 do not move time forward. They pile up points that push the same way: a second reason, a second merit, a second misfortune. それに is conversational; その上 is firmer and suits writing, often with まで or も ('even'), and is not followed by a request or invitation.

Do not use them as the 'and' between two nouns: 'books and pens' is 本とペン (only an afterthought item added with それから is fine). And none of them can carry a contrast or a result: if sentence two is unexpected, use でも; if it follows because of sentence one, use だから.
patterns: [point 1]。それに / その上、[another point the same way]。

examples.jp: 朝[あさ]ご飯[はん]を食[た]べました。{そして}、学校[がっこう]へ行[い]きました。
examples.en: I had breakfast. Then I went to school.

examples.jp: 宿題[しゅくだい]をします。{それから}、テレビを見[み]ます。
examples.en: I'll do my homework. After that, I'll watch TV.

examples.jp: この店[みせ]は安[やす]いです。{それに}、とてもおいしいです。
examples.en: This restaurant is cheap. Besides, the food is really good.

examples.jp: 卵[たまご]と牛乳[ぎゅうにゅう]、{それから}パンも買[か]ってきて。
examples.en: Get eggs and milk, and some bread as well.

examples.jp: 道[みち]に迷[まよ]った。{その上[うえ]}、雨[あめ]まで降[ふ]ってきた。
examples.en: I got lost. On top of that, it even started to rain.

contrast.note: しかし turns against sentence one ('however'). 安いです。それに、おいしいです adds a second good point; 安いです。しかし、まずいです sets a bad point against a good one.
だから says sentence two happens because of sentence one. 熱があった。だから休んだ is cause and result; そして would only report two events in a row.
それとも offers a choice in a question ('or'); the そして family adds things together ('and').

mistakes.bad: 駅[えき]に着[つ]きました。{それに}、電車[でんしゃ]に乗[の]りました。
mistakes.good: 駅[えき]に着[つ]きました。{それから}、電車[でんしゃ]に乗[の]りました。
mistakes.note: These are steps in time; それに piles up points and cannot mean 'and then'.

mistakes.bad: 本[ほん]{そして}ノートを買[か]いました。
mistakes.good: 本[ほん]{と}ノートを買[か]いました。
mistakes.note: そして links sentences or clauses, not two nouns; nouns are listed with と.

skills.tip: Ask: does time move on? そして / それから. Same point, one more reason? それに / その上.

skills.rule: でも, しかし, けれども and ところが open a sentence that goes against what the first one leads you to expect; ところが adds that the outcome was a surprise.
skills.explain:
All four mean 'but, however'. The difference is register: でも is everyday speech, けれども (shorter けれど, casual だけど) is spoken and a little softer, しかし is formal speech and writing (essays, news, speeches).

ところが is special. It reports a fact that turned out contrary to expectation: 'but, as it happened'. Sentence two must be something that actually happened or is the case, so ところが cannot introduce your own decision, request, invitation or opinion. 高い。でも買う ('but I'll buy it') is fine; 高い。ところが買う is not.

As connectors these words start a new sentence. Inside one sentence the contrast is carried by a particle on the verb: 降ったけれど, 降ったが, 降ったのに. 降ったでも is not Japanese.
patterns: [A]。でも / しかし / けれども、[contrary B]。

examples.jp: 日本語[にほんご]は難[むずか]しいです。{でも}、面白[おもしろ]いです。
examples.en: Japanese is hard. But it's interesting.

examples.jp: 一生懸命[いっしょうけんめい]走[はし]りました。{けれども}、電車[でんしゃ]に間[ま]に合[あ]いませんでした。
examples.en: I ran as fast as I could. But I didn't make the train.

examples.jp: この薬[くすり]はよく効[き]く。{しかし}、副作用[ふくさよう]も多[おお]い。
examples.en: This medicine works well. However, it also has many side effects.

examples.jp: 駅[えき]まで急[いそ]いだ。{ところが}、電車[でんしゃ]はもう出[で]た後[あと]だった。
examples.en: I hurried to the station. But the train had already gone.

examples.jp: 天気予報[てんきよほう]は晴[は]れだった。{ところが}、午後[ごご]から大雨[おおあめ]になった。
examples.en: The forecast said sunny. But, as it turned out, it poured from the afternoon.

contrast.note: だから is the opposite logic: B follows from A. 雨だった。だから行かなかった ('so I didn't go'); 雨だった。でも行った ('but I went').
そして adds without opposing. If sentence two would surprise someone who heard only sentence one, you need the でも family.
つまり restates sentence one in other words ('in other words'); it never sets up a contrast.

mistakes.bad: 雨[あめ]が降[ふ]った{でも}、出[で]かけました。
mistakes.good: 雨[あめ]が降[ふ]った{けれど}、出[で]かけました。
mistakes.note: でも as a connector opens a new sentence; inside one sentence attach けれど or が to the verb.

mistakes.bad: この服[ふく]は高[たか]い。{ところが}、買[か]うつもりだ。
mistakes.good: この服[ふく]は高[たか]い。{でも}、買[か]うつもりだ。
mistakes.note: ところが reports an unexpected fact; it cannot introduce your own decision.

skills.tip: Would sentence two surprise you after sentence one? Contrast family. Did it surprise you when it happened? ところが.

skills.rule: だから, それで and そのため open the result of sentence one; だから may be followed by a request, order, invitation or intention, それで may not.
skills.explain:
All three say 'so, therefore'. だから (polite ですから) states the result as the speaker's own reasoning, so it can be followed by anything: a fact, a decision, a request, an order. 明日は早いよ。だから、もう寝なさい.

それで ('and so, that's why') narrates a result that came about: 電車が遅れた。それで遅刻した. It is followed by facts, not by requests, invitations or 'let's'. In conversation それで? alone means 'and then?'.

そのため ('for that reason, because of this') is formal and written: news, reports, notices. It links an objective cause to an objective result.

Inside one sentence the cause takes the particle から or ので on the verb: 熱があるから休みます. だから, それで and そのため open a second sentence.

examples.jp: 熱[ねつ]があります。{だから}、今日[きょう]は休[やす]みます。
examples.en: I have a fever. So I'm taking today off.

examples.jp: 明日[あした]は早[はや]いよ。{だから}、もう寝[ね]なさい。
examples.en: You've got an early start tomorrow. So go to bed now.

examples.jp: 電車[でんしゃ]が遅[おく]れました。{それで}、会議[かいぎ]に遅刻[ちこく]しました。
examples.en: The train was late. That's why I was late for the meeting.

examples.jp: 道[みち]がわからなかった。{それで}、駅員[えきいん]さんに聞[き]いた。
examples.en: I didn't know the way. So I asked a station attendant.

examples.jp: 大雪[おおゆき]が降[ふ]った。{そのため}、多[おお]くの便[びん]が欠航[けっこう]した。
examples.en: There was heavy snow. Because of this, many flights were cancelled.

contrast.note: しかし sets sentence two against sentence one. 寒かった。だからコートを着た: the coat follows from the cold; しかし would mean the coat was against expectation.
それに adds a further point the same way ('besides'); it does not say that sentence two is caused by sentence one.
から and ので are particles on the end of the cause clause, inside one sentence: 熱があるから休みます. だから starts a new sentence.

mistakes.bad: 明日[あした]は試験[しけん]です。{それで}、早[はや]く寝[ね]てください。
mistakes.good: 明日[あした]は試験[しけん]です。{だから}、早[はや]く寝[ね]てください。
mistakes.note: それで narrates a result; a request after the reason needs だから.

mistakes.bad: 寒[さむ]かった。{しかし}、コートを着[き]た。
mistakes.good: 寒[さむ]かった。{だから}、コートを着[き]た。
mistakes.note: Putting on a coat is the natural result of the cold, not a contrast.

skills.tip: Can you insert 'because of that'? Result family. Is sentence two a request or a 'let's'? だから, never それで.

skills.rule: それとも is 'or' between two questions, asking the listener to pick one; または and あるいは are 'or' in statements, rules and instructions.
skills.explain:
それとも lives in questions. It joins two alternatives the listener must choose between, usually two full questions: コーヒーにしますか、それとも紅茶にしますか. In casual speech: 今日行く？それとも明日にする？

または is 'or' in statements, rules and instructions, typically between nouns: 黒または青のペンで書いてください. It means 'either one is acceptable'. In a question it asks whether either is possible (電話またはメールで連絡できますか), not which one you want.

あるいは is a more formal または, common in writing and announcements. It also has a second meaning, 'perhaps', with かもしれない: あるいは本当かもしれない.

In ordinary conversation, a plain 'A or B' between nouns is just the particle か: 明日か明後日.
patterns: [noun A] または / あるいは [noun B]  (statement, rule)
あるいは … かもしれない  ('perhaps')

examples.jp: コーヒーにしますか、{それとも}紅茶[こうちゃ]にしますか。
examples.en: Would you like coffee, or tea?

examples.jp: 黒[くろ]{または}青[あお]のペンで書[か]いてください。
examples.en: Please write in black or blue pen.

examples.jp: 今日[きょう]行[い]く？{それとも}明日[あした]にする？
examples.en: Shall we go today? Or make it tomorrow?

examples.jp: 申込書[もうしこみしょ]は郵送[ゆうそう]{または}メールで送[おく]ってください。
examples.en: Please send the application form by post or by email.

examples.jp: 会議[かいぎ]は月曜日[げつようび]{あるいは}火曜日[かようび]に行[おこな]われる予定[よてい]です。
examples.en: The meeting is scheduled for Monday or Tuesday.

examples.jp: 彼[かれ]の話[はなし]は、{あるいは}本当[ほんとう]かもしれない。
examples.en: What he says may perhaps be true.

contrast.note: The particle か is the everyday 'or' between nouns: 明日か明後日. または and あるいは are the formal, written versions; それとも is for choice questions.
そして means 'and': both things happen. または means 'or': one of them is enough.
だから gives a result, not an option; it never means 'or'.

mistakes.bad: 鉛筆[えんぴつ]{それとも}ボールペンで書[か]いてください。
mistakes.good: 鉛筆[えんぴつ]{または}ボールペンで書[か]いてください。
mistakes.note: An instruction is not a question; 'either is fine' is または.

mistakes.bad: 明日[あした]、{それとも}明後日[あさって]に行[い]きます。
mistakes.good: 明日[あした]{か}明後日[あさって]に行[い]きます。
mistakes.note: それとも needs a question; in a plain spoken statement 'A or B' is AかB.

skills.tip: Is there a question mark and must the listener pick? それとも. Otherwise または (formal: あるいは, casual: か).

skills.rule: それでは / じゃ move on from what has just been said ('well then'); ところで jumps to an unrelated topic ('by the way'); さて turns to the next step ('now then').
skills.explain:
それでは ('well then', polite) and its casual forms では and じゃ (じゃあ) close one stage and open the next because of what came before: everyone is here, so let's begin; that's all, so goodbye. They start classes and meetings and end conversations (じゃ、また明日). They also mean 'in that case': 雨ですか。じゃ、やめましょう.

ところで ('by the way') breaks off and raises something unrelated to what was just said, often after small talk. It does not end a conversation or follow logically from the previous point.

さて ('now, well now') marks a move to the next item in your own programme: the next part of a talk, the next job. It is common in presentations and narration, and alone when getting up to do something (さて、帰ろうか).

Do not confuse それでは with それで ('and so'), which gives a result.
patterns: [situation]。それでは / じゃ、[next step that follows from it]。

examples.jp: {じゃ}、また明日[あした]。
examples.en: Well then, see you tomorrow.

examples.jp: {それでは}、授業[じゅぎょう]を始[はじ]めます。
examples.en: Well then, let's begin the lesson.

examples.jp: 全員[ぜんいん]そろいましたね。{それでは}、出発[しゅっぱつ]しましょう。
examples.en: Everyone's here. Right then, let's set off.

examples.jp: いい天気[てんき]ですね。{ところで}、田中[たなか]さんはお元気[げんき]ですか。
examples.en: Lovely weather, isn't it? By the way, how is Mr Tanaka?

examples.jp: 昼[ひる]ご飯[はん]も食[た]べた。{さて}、仕事[しごと]に戻[もど]ろう。
examples.en: I've had lunch. Now then, back to work.

contrast.note: それで ('and so') states a result: 電車が遅れた。それで遅刻した. それでは ('well then') only moves the conversation on.
だから insists that sentence two follows as a reason-based result; それでは just signals the next stage.
それに adds another point to the same topic; ところで leaves the topic altogether.

mistakes.bad: 今日[きょう]はこれで終[お]わりです。{ところで}、また来週[らいしゅう]。
mistakes.good: 今日[きょう]はこれで終[お]わりです。{それでは}、また来週[らいしゅう]。
mistakes.note: Closing follows from 'that's all'; ところで would open a new topic, not say goodbye.

mistakes.bad: 寒[さむ]いですね。{じゃ}、お母[かあ]さんはお元気[げんき]ですか。
mistakes.good: 寒[さむ]いですね。{ところで}、お母[かあ]さんはお元気[げんき]ですか。
mistakes.note: Your mother's health does not follow from the cold; an unrelated topic needs ところで.

skills.tip: Follows from what was said: それでは / じゃ. Unrelated: ところで. Next item on my list: さて.
